posts.cooked:
Respected Sir/Ma’am,

I hope you are doing well.

As the System Commands end-term syllabus is quite extensive and spans both core and auxiliary topics, I wanted to request your guidance regarding topic prioritization for exam preparation.

From my understanding, topics like shell scripting, awk, sed, grep, regular expressions, pipelines, and cron scheduling form the core of the course. However, there are also several supporting topics such as hardware utilities, networking/SSH, version control concepts, prompt strings, and package/build utilities.

To prepare more effectively and avoid missing essential areas, could you please let us know:

  • which topics are must-not-skip for the end-term, and

  • which topics are mainly for conceptual awareness rather than detailed preparation?

This guidance would really help us focus our revision appropriately in the limited time available.

Thank you very much for your time and support.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
Thank you for your question.

For end-term preparation, you should prioritize the following must-not-skip topics, as they form the operational core of the course and are tested for correctness, reasoning, and command composition:

High-Priority (Must Prepare Thoroughly)

  • Shell fundamentals: command execution, exit status, chaining (&&, ||)
  • I/O redirection and pipelines
  • File and directory operations, permissions
  • grep, sed, awk (filters, substitutions, conditionals, aggregation)
  • Regular expressions (basic + extended, practical usage)
  • Archiving and compression (tar, gzip, related flags)
  • Sorting, uniqueness, counting (sort, uniq, wc)
  • Shell scripting basics:
    • Variables, quoting ("$@" vs "$*")
    • Loops, conditionals, functions
    • Exit codes and error handling
  • Cron jobs and scheduling syntax

Medium Priority (Prepare Conceptually + Basic Usage)

  • Prompt customization (PS1, environment variables)
  • Text processing utilities (cut, tr, paste, xargs)
  • Process management (ps, top, kill, job control)
  • Log handling and redirection patterns
  • Basic networking commands (ping, ssh, scp)
  • Environment variables and shell startup files

Conceptual Awareness (Know What/Why, Not Deep Syntax)

  • Package managers and build tools (apt/yum, make – high level)
  • Version control concepts (basic Git ideas, not workflows)
  • Hardware and system utilities (disk, memory, CPU tools – overview)
  • Filesystem hierarchy and Linux boot concepts

Additionally Recommended (Even if not emphasized earlier)

  • Quoting and globbing rules
  • Differences between GNU vs POSIX behavior (where relevant)
  • Safe scripting practices (idempotency, avoiding destructive commands)
  • Reading and understanding man pages effectively

Focus first on correctness and reasoning with commands, then on composing multi-step pipelines and scripts. Breadth matters, but depth in core Unix text processing and shell behavior is essential.

Best wishes for your preparation.
